results.title: Successor criterion for monotone sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a preordered set. A sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ is monotone (that is, $f(m) \le f(n)$ whenever $m \le n$) if and only if $f(n) \le f(n+1)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Successor criterion for antitone sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a preordered set. A sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ is antitone (that is, $f(n) \le f(m)$ whenever $m \le n$) if and only if $f(n+1) \le f(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Successor criterion for monotone or antitone sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a preordered set and let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be a sequence. Then $f$ is monotone ($f(m) \le f(n)$ whenever $m \le n$) or antitone ($f(n) \le f(m)$ whenever $m \le n$) if and only if either $f(n) \le f(n+1)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, or $f(n+1) \le f(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Ribes' question on generator counts (Kourovka 12.71)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $d(X)$ for the minimal number of generators of a finite group $X$. This is the proposition that for all finite groups $A$ and $B$ there are a finite group $G$ and subgroups $H, K \le G$ with $H \cong A$, $K \cong B$ and $\langle H, K \rangle = G$ such that $d(G) = d(A) + d(B)$.

results.title: Generator counts of groups generated by two subgroups are not always additive (Kourovka 12.71)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $d(X)$ for the minimal number of generators of a finite group $X$. There are finite groups $A$ and $B$ such that for every finite group $G$ and all subgroups $H, K \le G$ with $H \cong A$, $K \cong B$ and $\langle H, K \rangle = G$, we have $d(G) \ne d(A) + d(B)$.

results.title: Triangularization of an endomorphism with split characteristic polynomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$, let $f$ be an endomorphism of $V$ whose characteristic polynomial splits over $K$, and let $\iota$ be a finite linearly ordered set with exactly $\dim_K V$ elements. Then there is a basis $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $f$ is upper triangular: its $(i, j)$ entry is $0$ whenever $j < i$.

results.title: Triangularization of a matrix with split characteristic polynomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, let $n$ be a finite linearly ordered index set, and let $A$ be a square matrix over $K$ with rows and columns indexed by $n$ whose characteristic polynomial splits over $K$. Then there are an invertible matrix $P$ and a matrix $T$, both over $K$ and indexed by $n$, such that $T$ is upper triangular ($T_{ij} = 0$ whenever $j < i$) and $A = P T P^{-1}$.

results.title: Ramanujan's integrals of $\cos^n x \sin nx$ for every $n \ge 0$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k$ be the $n$-th harmonic number. Then $x \cos^n x \sin(nx)$ and $\cos^n x \sin(nx)$ are integrable on $[0, \pi/2]$, $\int_0^{\pi/2} x \cos^n x \sin(nx)\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2^{n+2}} H_n$ and $\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^n x \sin(nx)\,dx = \frac{1}{2^{n+1}} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{2^k}{k}$.

results.title: Gaussian binomial coefficient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring and $Q \in R$. For natural numbers $M$ and $k$, the Gaussian binomial coefficient $\binom{M}{k}_Q \in R$ is defined recursively by $\binom{M}{0}_Q = 1$, $\binom{0}{k+1}_Q = 0$ and $\binom{M+1}{k+1}_Q = \binom{M}{k}_Q + Q^{k+1} \binom{M}{k+1}_Q$.

part.title: Eulerian circuits
api: Edge list of an indexed walk
Edge list of an extended indexed walk

results.title: Edges at a vertex of an Eulerian trail
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and let $p$ be an Eulerian trail in $G$, that is, a walk between any two vertices that uses every edge of $G$ exactly once. Then for every vertex $x$, the number of edges of $p$ that contain $x$, counted with multiplicity along $p$, equals the degree of $x$ in $G$.

results.title: Euler circuits in connected even graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite connected simple graph in which every vertex has even degree has a closed Eulerian trail, that is, a closed walk that uses every edge of the graph exactly once.

results.title: Reachability among non-isolated vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and let $u$ and $v$ be non-isolated vertices of $G$, that is, vertices with at least one neighbour. If $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $G$, then $v$ is reachable from $u$ in the subgraph of $G$ induced on the set of non-isolated vertices.

results.title: Euler circuits in simple graphs whose non-isolated vertices are connected
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph in which every vertex has even degree, and suppose that the subgraph of $G$ induced on its non-isolated vertices is connected (in particular nonempty, so $G$ has at least one edge). Then $G$ has a closed Eulerian trail, that is, a closed walk that uses every edge of $G$ exactly once.

results.title: Edge-indexed multigraph
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An edge-indexed multigraph with vertex type $V$ and edge type $E$ assigns to each edge $e \in E$ an unordered pair of endpoints in $V$, such that no edge has two equal endpoints. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints, so parallel edges are distinguished by their elements of $E$.

results.title: Indexed walk
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph, an indexed walk is a walk that records which edge it traverses at each step. Indexed walks are defined inductively: for every vertex $v$ there is the empty indexed walk from $v$ to $v$, and if $e$ is an edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$ and $p$ is an indexed walk from $v$ to $w$, then traversing $e$ from $u$ to $v$ and then following $p$ is an indexed walk from $u$ to $w$.

results.title: Vertex list of an indexed walk
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The support of an indexed walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in an edge-indexed multigraph is the list of the vertices that $p$ visits, in order and with repetitions, including both endpoints: the empty walk at $w$ has support $[w]$, and a walk that starts at $u$ with an edge and continues with an indexed walk $q$ has support $u$ followed by the support of $q$.

results.title: Edge list of an indexed walk
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The edge list of an indexed walk is the list of the edge identities it traverses, in order and with repetitions: the empty walk has the empty edge list, and the walk that traverses an edge $e$ and then follows an indexed walk $p$ has edge list $e$ followed by the edge list of $p$.

results.title: Indexed trail
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An indexed walk $p$ in an edge-indexed multigraph is a trail when its edge list has no repeated entries, that is, $p$ traverses each edge of the multigraph at most once.

results.title: Characterization of indexed trails
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An indexed walk is a trail exactly when its edge list has no duplicates.

results.title: Eulerian indexed walk
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An indexed walk is Eulerian when it is a trail, that is, it uses no edge identity twice, and every edge identity of the multigraph occurs in its edge list.

results.title: Characterization of Eulerian indexed walks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An indexed walk is Eulerian exactly when it is a trail whose edge list contains every edge identity of the multigraph.

results.title: Support of the empty indexed walk
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The support of the empty indexed walk at a vertex $v$ is the one-element list $[v]$.

results.title: Support of a walk extended at the front
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $e$ is an edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$ and $p$ is an indexed walk starting at $v$, then the support of the walk that traverses $e$ from $u$ to $v$ and then follows $p$ is $u$ followed by the support of $p$.

results.title: The empty indexed walk has no edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every vertex $v$ of an edge-indexed multigraph, the edge list of the empty indexed walk at $v$ is the empty list.

results.title: Edge list of an extended indexed walk
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be an indexed walk from $v$ to $w$ in an edge-indexed multigraph $M$, and let $e$ be an edge of $M$ with endpoints $u$ and $v$. The edge list of the walk from $u$ to $w$ that traverses $e$ and then follows $p$ is $e$ followed by the edge list of $p$.

results.title: Incidence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph, a vertex $v$ is incident with an edge $e$ when $v$ belongs to the unordered pair of endpoints of $e$.

results.title: Incidence is membership in the endpoint pair
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph, a vertex $v$ is incident with an edge $e$ if and only if $v$ belongs to the unordered pair of endpoints of $e$.

results.title: Underlying simple graph of an edge-indexed multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The underlying simple graph of an edge-indexed multigraph $M$ with vertex set $V$ is the simple graph on $V$ whose edges are the unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ that are the endpoint pair of some edge of $M$; such pairs have $u \ne v$ because $M$ is loopless. It forgets edge multiplicities.

results.title: Adjacency in the underlying graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph. Two vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the underlying simple graph of $M$ if and only if some edge $e$ of $M$ has endpoint pair $\{u, v\}$.

results.title: From an indexed walk to a walk in the underlying graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph. An indexed walk $p$ in $M$ from $u$ to $v$ yields a walk from $u$ to $v$ in the underlying simple graph of $M$ by forgetting edge identities: the empty indexed walk at $w$ goes to the empty walk at $w$, and an indexed walk that first traverses an edge $e$ with endpoints $\{u, x\}$ and then continues with an indexed walk $q$ goes to the walk that first steps from $u$ to $x$, an…

results.title: Forgetting edge identities preserves the vertex sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph and $p$ an indexed walk in $M$ from $u$ to $v$. The walk from $u$ to $v$ in the underlying simple graph of $M$ obtained from $p$ by forgetting edge identities visits the same vertices as $p$, in the same order: the two supports are equal as lists.

results.title: Edges of the forgetful walk
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every indexed walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in an edge-indexed multigraph, the edge list of the walk in the underlying simple graph obtained from $p$ by forgetting edge identities is the list of the endpoint pairs of the edges of $p$, taken in the same order.

results.title: Forgetting edge identities preserves length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an indexed walk $p$, the walk in the underlying simple graph obtained by forgetting edge identities has the same length as $p$, namely the number of entries in the edge list of $p$.

results.title: Degree in an edge-indexed multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The degree of a vertex $v$ in an edge-indexed multigraph $M$ is the number of edges of $M$ incident with $v$, that is, the cardinality of the set of edges whose endpoint pair contains $v$; it is defined to be $0$ when this set is infinite.

results.title: Degree as the number of incident edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every vertex $v$ of an edge-indexed multigraph $M$, the degree of $v$ equals the cardinality of the set of edges of $M$ whose endpoint pair contains $v$, where this cardinality is taken to be $0$ when the set is infinite.

results.title: Disjoint sum of edge-indexed multigraphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given edge-indexed multigraphs $M$ and $N$ on the same vertex type $V$, with edge types $E$ and $F$, their disjoint sum is the edge-indexed multigraph on $V$ whose edge type is the disjoint union $E \sqcup F$, where an edge coming from $E$ has its endpoints in $M$ and an edge coming from $F$ has its endpoints in $N$.

results.title: Endpoints of edges from the first summand
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type. Every edge $e$ of $M$, viewed as an edge of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$, has the same endpoints as in $M$.

results.title: Endpoints of edges from the second summand
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type. Every edge $f$ of $N$, viewed as an edge of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$, has the same endpoints as in $N$.

results.title: Degrees add under disjoint sums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type, each with finitely many edges. Then for every vertex $v$, the degree of $v$ in the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$ equals the degree of $v$ in $M$ plus the degree of $v$ in $N$.

results.title: Adding edges preserves connectedness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type. If the underlying simple graph of $M$ is connected, then the underlying simple graph of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$ is connected.

results.title: Handshake lemma for edge-indexed multigraphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is even.

results.title: Euler circuits in edge-indexed multigraphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. If the underlying simple graph of $M$ is connected and every vertex of $M$ has even degree, then there are a vertex $u$ and a closed indexed walk from $u$ to $u$ that is Eulerian, that is, it traverses every edge of $M$ exactly once.

results.title: Euler circuits in edge-indexed multigraphs whose non-isolated vertices are connected
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. Suppose that the subgraph of the underlying simple graph of $M$ induced on its non-isolated vertices is connected, and that every vertex of $M$ has even degree. Then there are a vertex $u$ and a closed indexed walk from $u$ to $u$ that is Eulerian, that is, it traverses every edge of $M$ exactly once.

results.title: Line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph is the simple graph whose vertices are the edge identities, two of them being adjacent when they are distinct and share an endpoint. In particular, parallel edges are adjacent.

results.title: Adjacency in the line graph of a multigraph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Two edge identities $e_1$ and $e_2$ are adjacent in the line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph exactly when $e_1 \ne e_2$ and some vertex is incident with both of them.

results.title: Maximum degree of a multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edge identities, the maximum degree is the largest degree of a vertex, and $0$ when there are no vertices.

results.title: Degrees are bounded by the maximum degree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. Then every vertex of $M$ has degree at most the maximum degree of $M$.

results.title: Degree counts incident edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many edges, the degree of every vertex $v$ equals the number of edges incident with $v$.

results.title: Alphabet preimage
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage of $L$ under $f$ is the language over $\Sigma$ consisting of the words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ such that $f(a_1) f(a_2) \cdots f(a_n) \in L$.

results.title: Alphabet preimage morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage morphism of $f$ and $L$ is the monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends a word $w$ to the syntactic class of $f^*(w)$, the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. It is the composite of the letterwise map $f^* \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$…

results.title: The alphabet preimage morphism recognizes the alphabet preimage
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write $f^*(w)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of a word $w$, $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $A_L \subseteq M(L)$ for the accepting set of classes of words in $L$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the alphabet preimage morphism…

results.title: Syntactic equivalence pulls back along an alphabet map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$, and $K$ the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. If $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are words such that $f^*(x)$ and $f^*(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $K$.

results.title: The alphabet preimage morphism refines the preimage's syntactic congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ with syntactic monoid $M(L)$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ the alphabet preimage morphism, which sends a word $w$ to the class in $M(L)$ of the word $f^*(w)$ obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically congruent…

results.title: Division map for the syntactic monoid of an alphabet preimage
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write $f^*(w)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of a word $w$, $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $K$ for the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the alphabet preimage morphism…

results.title: Alphabet preimages preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then the syntactic monoid of the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ is finite, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$.

results.title: Regular languages are closed under alphabet preimages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets. If $L$ is a regular language over $\Gamma$, then its alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ is regular, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$.

results.title: Renaming letters by a bijection preserves and reflects regularity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a bijection between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid e^*(w) \in L\}$, where $e^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $e$ to each letter of $w$, is regular if and only if $L$ is regular.

results.title: Finiteness of the syntactic monoid is invariant under renaming letters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a bijection between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The syntactic monoid of the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid e^*(w) \in L\}$, where $e^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $e$ to each letter of $w$, is finite if and only if the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.

results.title: Inverse image under a word morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\Sigma$ and $\Gamma$ be alphabets, $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ a monoid morphism between their free monoids of words, and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The inverse image of $L$ under $h$ is the language $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ over $\Sigma$.

results.title: Word morphisms act letter by letter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids. For every word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Sigma^*$ (including the empty word, $n = 0$), we have $h(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n) = h(a_1) h(a_2) \cdots h(a_n)$, the concatenation of the images of its letters.

results.title: Letterwise description of the inverse image under a word morphism
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ consists exactly of the words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Sigma^*$ such that the concatenation $h(a_1) h(a_2) \cdots h(a_n)$ of the images of their letters lies in $L$.

results.title: Recognizing morphism of an inverse image
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ with syntactic monoid $M(L)$. The recognizing morphism of $h$ and $L$ is the monoid morphism $\Sigma^* \to M(L)$ that sends a word $w$ to the syntactic class $[h(w)]_L$ of $h(w)$; it is the composite of $h$ with the syntactic morphism of $L$.

results.title: Syntactic equivalence pulls back along a word morphism
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$, and $K = h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ its inverse image. If $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are words such that $h(x)$ and $h(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $K$.

results.title: Division map for the syntactic monoid of an inverse image
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $K$ for the inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the recognizing morphism $w \mapsto [h(w)]_L$. This is the monoid morphism from the submonoid…

results.title: Inverse images under word morphisms preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then the syntactic monoid of the inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ is finite.

results.title: Regular languages are closed under inverse word morphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids. If $L$ is a regular language over $\Gamma$, then its inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ is regular.

results.title: Alphabet preimages are inverse images under word morphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $f^* \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ the monoid morphism that applies $f$ to each letter of a word, and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Then the alphabet preimage of $L$ under $f$ equals the inverse image $(f^*)^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ of $L$ under $f^*$.

part.title: Fixation and absorption in the Wright–Fisher diffusion

path: Fixation and absorption in the Wright–Fisher diffusion

results.title: Martingale problem for the Wright–Fisher diffusion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `X` solves the martingale problem for the Wright–Fisher diffusion with scaled genic selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns` (time in units of `2N` generations) with respect to the filtration `ℱ` and the measure `μ`: `X` takes values in `[0, 1]`, has continuous paths, is adapted to `ℱ`, and for every `C²` function `f` the process `f (X t) - f (X 0) - ∫₀ᵗ generator σ f (X s) ds` is an `ℱ`-martingale.

results.title: Absorption time of a frequency path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The absorption time of a `[0, 1]`-valued path: the first time it is at `0` or `1` (the infimum of the empty set is `0` in `ℝ≥0`; the path is absorbed almost surely, see `ae_exists_absorbed`).

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability is twice continuously differentiable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is a `C²` function of the initial frequency on all of `ℝ`.

results.title: Positivity of Kimura's slope constant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The slope constant of Kimura's formula is positive.

results.title: Strict monotonicity of Kimura's fixation probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is strictly increasing in the initial frequency.

results.title: Absorption in finite time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A solution of the Wright–Fisher martingale problem is almost surely absorbed: from some time on it is constantly `0` or constantly `1`.

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability, process form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a solution of the Wright–Fisher martingale problem with scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns` started at frequency `x`, the probability that the allele is eventually fixed is `(1 - e^{-2σx}) / (1 - e^{-2σ})` (`x` when `σ = 0`).

results.title: Kimura–Ohta mean absorption time, process form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a solution of the neutral Wright–Fisher martingale problem started at frequency `x`, the expected time to loss or fixation, in units of `2N` generations, is `-2 (x log x + (1 - x) log (1 - x))`.

results.title: Admixture graph
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An admixture graph on the nodes `V` (Patterson et al. 2012): a rooted directed acyclic graph in which every non-root node has one or two parents, with admixture proportions.

results.title: Edges of an admixture graph
results.caption: Abbreviation

results.title: Probability that a lineage passes through a node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `visit X c` is the probability that the lineage of a gene sampled in `X`, traced toward the root with parents chosen according to the admixture proportions, passes through `c`.

results.title: Lineage weight of an edge in an admixture graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `weight X e` is the probability that the lineage of a gene sampled in `X` traverses the edge `e = (c, p)`: it reaches `c` and then descends from `p`.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The probability of a root-ward path `[v₀, v₁, …, v_k]`: the product of the proportions `prop vᵢ vᵢ₊₁`.

results.title: Root-ward paths from a node of an admixture graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The root-ward paths from `X`: the lists `[X = v₀, v₁, …, v_k = root]` with each `vᵢ₊₁` a parent of `vᵢ`.

results.caption: Theorem

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A lineage passes through its own node with probability `1`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of visit probabilities
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Visit probabilities are at most one

results.summary: Visit probabilities are at most `1`.

results.title: Every lineage reaches the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every lineage reaches the root.

results.title: First-step equation for root-ward paths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: First-step equation for `paths`.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Admixture proportions are at most `1`.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Acyclicity: a lineage from a parent `Y` of `X` never passes through `X`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of lineage weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Lineage weights are nonnegative.

results.title: Lineage weights are at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Lineage weights are at most `1`.

results.title: First-step recursion for lineage weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: First-step recursion for lineage weights: a lineage from `X` traverses `e` either as its first step (if `e` starts at `X`) or after moving to a parent `Y`, chosen with probability `prop X Y`.

results.title: Lineage weight recursion at an admixture node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The recursion at an admixture node `X` with parents `A ≠ B`: with `α = prop X A`, `w X = α w A + (1 - α) w B + w₀`, where `w₀` puts weight `α` on the edge `(X, A)`, `1 - α` on `(X, B)` and `0` elsewhere.

results.title: Lineage weight recursion at a tree node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The recursion at a tree node `X` with the single parent `Y`: `w X = w Y + 1_{(X, Y)}`.

results.title: Path-sum formula for lineage weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Path-sum form of the lineage weights (Patterson et al. 2012): `weight X e` is the sum, over the root-ward paths from `X` that traverse `e`, of the products of the admixture proportions along the path.

results.title: Tree-shaped admixture graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The graph is a tree: no node has two parents.

results.title: Visit probabilities on a tree are zero or one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On a tree every visit probability is `0` or `1`.

results.title: Lineage weights on a tree are zero or one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On a tree every lineage weight is `0` or `1`.

results.title: Drift model of an admixture graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The drift model of an admixture graph: the populations are the nodes, the root frequency is `root`, the edge increments are `incr` (square integrable and pairwise uncorrelated), the drift length of an edge is the second moment of its increment, and the weights are the lineage weights of the graph.

results.title: A tree-shaped admixture graph has binary loadings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A tree-shaped admixture graph induces a drift model with binary loadings (all weights `0` or `1`).

results.title: Three-population test is nonnegative on a tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The three-population test on a tree-shaped admixture graph: `f3 C A B ≥ 0`.

results.title: Three-population statistic at an admixture node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The three-population statistic at an admixture node `X` with parents `A ≠ B`, proportions `α = prop X A` and `β = prop X B` (`α + β = 1`), in a drift model with the graph's weights: `f3 X A B = α² ℓ_{XA} + β² ℓ_{XB} - α β f2 A B`, where `ℓ_{XA}`, `ℓ_{XB}` are the drift lengths of the two admixture edges.

results.title: Three-population statistic at an admixture node without edge drift
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With no drift on the admixture edges, an admixture node `X` with parents `A ≠ B` and proportion `α = prop X A` has `f3 X A B = -α (1 - α) f2 A B` (the hypothesis of the seed's `DriftModel.f3_admixture`, here derived from the graph).
